note: Rule cards of the cafe pack that no game record links to by id: knowledge for the advisor (ai/src/advisor.ts). Same shape as pack.ruleCards. Built by packs/next/build.mjs.

ruleCards.title: Rent starts before sales do
ruleCards.text: NYC restaurant leases usually give 3-6 months of free rent. Renovating a former restaurant takes 3-5 months, an empty shell 6-9, and brokers count 8-12 months from signing to opening. Every month past the free period is rent with no income.

ruleCards.title: Good guy guarantee
ruleCards.text: Under a "good guy" guarantee you personally owe the rent only until you hand back the keys: notice given, rent paid, space empty and clean. New York's top court confirmed in 2025 that liability stops on the day you leave.

ruleCards.title: How big the deposit gets
ruleCards.text: There is no legal cap on a commercial deposit. Brokers see 3-6 months of rent for tenants with credit and 6-12 months for startups and restaurants, often as a bank letter of credit that takes 2-3 weeks to issue and costs about 1-2% a year.

ruleCards.title: Rent goes up every year
ruleCards.text: Most NYC retail leases raise base rent by a fixed percentage each year, typically about 3%, compounding: $100 per square foot in year one is about $130 in year ten. Ask whether the increase is simple or compound before you sign.

ruleCards.title: You pay the landlord's tax increases
ruleCards.text: Most NYC store leases make the tenant pay a share of any rise in the building's property tax above a base year. If the base year is low, a reassessment lands on you: brokers see $10-$20 per square foot a year added in older buildings.

ruleCards.title: Staying past the lease
ruleCards.text: If you stay after the lease ends without a renewal, the holdover clause applies: typically 150% to 200% of the last rent, and New York courts enforce it. A commercial tenant has no legal right to renew.

ruleCards.title: Selling does not free you from the lease
ruleCards.text: When you sell and assign your lease, you stay liable for the rent unless the landlord releases you in writing, even if the landlord consented and takes rent from the buyer. Selling a majority of your LLC can count as an assignment too.

ruleCards.title: Who pays the broker
ruleCards.text: In New York City retail leasing the landlord normally pays one full brokerage commission, split between its broker and yours, so a tenant's broker costs you nothing directly. It is priced into the rent.

ruleCards.title: Free lease lawyer
ruleCards.text: The city's Commercial Lease Assistance Program reviews and negotiates leases for eligible small businesses at no charge and calls back within 3 business days. It served 812 businesses in the year to June 2025. It will not represent you in court.

ruleCards.title: Empty storefronts are leverage
ruleCards.text: About 11% of New York City storefronts were vacant in April 2026: 12.9% in Manhattan, 12.3% in Brooklyn, 9.5% in Queens, and 21% in the Financial District. A landlord with a store empty for a year will trade free rent for a signed lease.

ruleCards.title: Stop Work Order
ruleCards.text: Working against a Stop Work Order costs $6,000 the first time and $12,000 each time after. The Department of Buildings does not lift the order until the penalties are paid, and rent keeps running on the idle site.

ruleCards.title: What needs no permit
ruleCards.text: Painting, plastering, new cabinets, resurfacing floors and swapping a plumbing fixture need no Buildings permit. Moving a wall, a drain or a gas line does, with plans filed by a registered architect or engineer.

ruleCards.title: How long a Buildings permit takes
ruleCards.text: In 2025 the Department of Buildings finished a first plan review in 3.7 business days on average and took 20.3 days from application to approval; early in fiscal 2026 that rose to 23.6 days. Objections from the examiner restart the clock.

ruleCards.title: Asbestos report before any permit
ruleCards.text: For work in a building put up before April 1, 1987, the Buildings permit is not issued until a certified asbestos investigator files an ACP-5 report. Only buildings newer than that can claim the exemption.

ruleCards.title: Storefronts in historic districts
ruleCards.text: In a historic district every exterior change to a storefront needs a Landmarks permit first. Staff approve complete applications in 10-15 business days, and 95% of approvals never go to a hearing. The fee is $95 for the first $25,000 of work.

ruleCards.title: Waiting for gas
ruleCards.text: A 2017 State Senate survey of city restaurants found an average wait of 68 days for gas service; only 17% were served on time and one waited over a year. The delays cost each business an average of $140,000.

ruleCards.title: Sales tax on your build-out
ruleCards.text: New York presumes work done for a tenant is temporary and taxable at 8.875%. If the lease gives the improvements to the landlord and does not make you remove them, hand the contractor a Certificate of Capital Improvement (Form ST-124): the labor is tax-free.

ruleCards.title: A worker falls on your job
ruleCards.text: New York Labor Law §240 makes owners absolutely liable when a construction worker falls. Courts treat the tenant who hired the contractor as an owner. Before work starts, get insurance certificates that name you and the landlord.

ruleCards.title: Your contractor's unpaid bills
ruleCards.text: A subcontractor your contractor did not pay can file a mechanic's lien on the property for up to 8 months after its last work. Most leases make that your default. Clearing it takes a bond of 110% of the claim. Collect lien waivers with every payment.

ruleCards.title: Utility deposit
ruleCards.text: Con Edison requires a security deposit from a new business customer: up to two times the average monthly bill, estimated from a similar business. You may pay half at first and ask for the amount to be reviewed.

ruleCards.title: A free city project manager
ruleCards.text: Executive Order 18 of July 2026 tells Small Business Services to give each client of the NYC Business Express Service Team a project manager who identifies permits, helps apply and coordinates pre-opening inspections. The service is free.

ruleCards.title: Permits do not come with the shop
ruleCards.text: Under NYC Health Code §5.11 a food permit is void the moment it is transferred to anyone not named on it. A buyer applies for a new one and may open on the 22nd day after applying. Liquor and sidewalk-cafe licenses do not transfer either.

ruleCards.title: Sales tax on a bought business
ruleCards.text: When you buy a shop you pay 8.875% sales tax on the furniture, fixtures and equipment part of the price, though not on inventory for resale, goodwill or the lease. How the contract splits the price decides the bill.

ruleCards.title: What a coffee shop sells for
ruleCards.text: US coffee shops and cafes sold between 2021 and 2025 went for a median 0.41 times yearly revenue and 2.0 times the owner's yearly earnings; the middle half fell between 1.5 and 2.55 times earnings. The median sale price in 2025 was $176,500.

ruleCards.title: You inherit the seller's unemployment record
ruleCards.text: When you buy all or part of a business in New York, the seller's unemployment-insurance experience account transfers to you and your rate is recalculated from the transfer date. Not reporting the purchase does not prevent it.

ruleCards.title: Borrowing to buy a business
ruleCards.text: An SBA 7(a) loan to start or buy a business requires at least 10% of the project cost from the buyer. A seller note can cover at most half of that, and only if the seller takes no payments for the whole loan term.

ruleCards.title: The 14-day rule for franchises
ruleCards.text: Federal rules give you the franchise disclosure document 14 calendar days before you sign or pay; New York law says at least 10 business days, and the offering must be registered with the state Attorney General before it is sold.

ruleCards.title: What a coffee franchise takes
ruleCards.text: Gregorys Coffee charges a $35,000 fee, a 6% royalty and 2.5% for marketing on a $459,000-$946,000 investment. Dunkin' charges $40,000, 5.9% plus 5% for advertising, and expects $250,000 in liquid assets and $500,000 net worth.

ruleCards.title: Vending without a license
ruleCards.text: Selling food from a cart with no license or no permit decal starts at $1,000 per summons in New York City, and a cart with no licensed vendor at it can be seized and forfeited.

ruleCards.title: Cart permits are capped
ruleCards.text: New year-round food cart permits go only to holders of a supervisory license from a waiting list. The city adds 2,200 a year in fiscal 2027-2031: 500 citywide, 1,500 outside Manhattan, 200 for veterans and disabled people. Renewal is $438 every two years.

ruleCards.title: A cart needs a commissary
ruleCards.text: Every food cart must be stored at a Health Department-permitted commissary and return there at least once a day for cleaning and supplies. No commissary agreement, no permit. Guides quote $300-$1,200 a month.

ruleCards.title: Pop-ups need a permit too
ruleCards.text: A stand at a street fair or market needs a $70 Temporary Food Service Establishment permit, good for events of 14 days or less, one event at a time. Without it the stand is closed on the spot and fined $200 to $2,000.

ruleCards.title: A kiosk in a park
ruleCards.text: A park cafe or kiosk is a city concession won through a public request for proposals. The operator pays the higher of a minimum yearly fee or a share of gross receipts: a 2024 award for a cafe in a Manhattan park set $40,000 against 4%, rising 5% a year.

ruleCards.title: Sick leave balances survive a sale
ruleCards.text: When a New York City business is sold, workers who stay keep their unused safe and sick leave with the new owner. The buyer must hand out its written policy at the sale, and seller and buyer are jointly liable if balances are not carried over.

ruleCards.title: As-is, white box or turnkey
ruleCards.text: A lease says in what state the landlord delivers the room: as-is, a "white box" shell with a panel, plumbing stubs and basic air conditioning, or turnkey. Any construction allowance is usually repaid after the work is done, so you fund it first.

ruleCards.title: The 22-day clock starts when you apply
ruleCards.text: You may open on the 22nd day after submitting the food permit application, even with no inspection; the inspector then comes unannounced after you open. The city advises applying early: three weeks before the room is finished costs nothing.

ruleCards.title: The black market in cart permits
ruleCards.text: A two-year cart permit costs $75-$200 from the city, but the cap means vendors rent them from holders for $6,000 to $25,000. Renting is illegal for both sides: permits are not transferable, and the renter is an unpermitted vendor.

ruleCards.title: Who pays the business broker
ruleCards.text: When a small business is sold through a broker, the seller pays the success fee, usually 8-15% of the price, at closing. Sellers price it in. Two to four weeks of training by the seller are normally part of the deal; ask for it in writing.

ruleCards.title: A noise plan on the wall of the site
ruleCards.text: Every construction site in the city, a cafe renovation included, must post a Construction Noise Mitigation Plan where inspectors can see it at all times. It is not filed with anyone, just posted. Without it a neighbor's noise complaint becomes a fine.

ruleCards.title: A certificate for the gas cylinders
ruleCards.text: Soda guns and other compressed-gas setups need a staff member with a Fire Department Certificate of Fitness (G-46): $25, valid 3 years, $15 to renew. Operating without the required certificate is fined $1,000 to $5,000.

ruleCards.title: Zoning comes before the lease
ruleCards.text: A cafe is legal only where zoning allows it. Since June 2024 the city lets a vacant storefront on a residential block be reused without a 2-year deadline, but only for neighborhood uses. Check the address on the city's zoning map first.

ruleCards.title: One free team for all the agencies
ruleCards.text: The NYC Business Express Service Team gives small businesses free one-on-one help: getting licenses and permits faster, preparing for inspections and fixing issues beforehand. Call 888-SBS-4NYC. In July 2026 the mayor ordered a project manager for each client.

ruleCards.title: The 75-person line
ruleCards.text: A room for fewer than 75 people, staff included, is business space and one exit can serve up to 74. At 75 it is a place of assembly: second exit, outward-swinging doors, a Buildings certificate and a yearly Fire Department permit. People are counted, not chairs.

ruleCards.title: How the code counts people
ruleCards.text: The building code counts one person per 15 sq ft where there are tables and chairs and one per 5 sq ft where people stand. A 70 sq ft queue area counts as 14 people, so a crowded line can take a room over its limit before the seats do.

ruleCards.title: Over capacity
ruleCards.text: More people inside than the Certificate of Occupancy allows is an immediately hazardous violation: $2,500, or $12,500 if you miss the hearing, and it cannot be cured with paperwork. For one big night, a temporary permit costs $250, filed 10 business days ahead.

ruleCards.title: The cellar is storage
ruleCards.text: A cellar listed as storage on the Certificate of Occupancy may hold stock, not customers. Seating down there is "occupancy contrary to the Certificate": $1,250, or $6,250 on default. Making it legal means exits, ceiling height and an amended certificate.

ruleCards.title: Access inside the room
ruleCards.text: At least 5% of your seats must work from a wheelchair: a table top 28 to 34 inches high with knee room, on a route at least 36 inches wide. The order counter needs a section at least 36 inches long and no higher than 36 inches. Doors need 32 inches of clear width.

ruleCards.title: The government shares the cost of access
ruleCards.text: A business with sales of $1 million or less, or no more than 30 full-time workers, gets a federal credit for ramps, doors and restroom changes: 50% of what it spends between $250 and $10,250 a year, up to $5,000 (IRS Form 8826).

ruleCards.title: What an awning may say
ruleCards.text: An awning is a permitted job, and zoning limits its text: the shop's name and address, letters no taller than 12 inches, no more than 12 sq ft of lettering. Photos, menus and phone numbers printed on the fabric are what inspectors cite.

ruleCards.title: Roll-down gates
ruleCards.text: A 2009 law told shops to have gates at least 70% see-through by July 1, 2026; owners were quoted $6,000 to $7,000 a gate. The Council dropped the deadline 51-0 on June 30, 2026. The 70% rule now applies only to a new or replaced gate.

ruleCards.title: How much sidewalk you can use
ruleCards.text: A sidewalk cafe must leave walkers half the sidewalk or 8 feet, whichever is more (10 feet on regional corridors, 12 on global ones), and stay 15 feet from a subway stair. On a 12-foot side-street sidewalk that leaves one row of small tables at most.

ruleCards.title: What outdoor seats cost
ruleCards.text: License $1,050 for four years; refundable deposit $1,500 (sidewalk) or $2,500 (roadway); roadway hearing notice $500-$900; then $6 to $31 per sq ft a year by sector. The city's own example: 120 sq ft of sidewalk costs $720 a year in most of the city, $3,720 in central Manhattan.

ruleCards.title: Roadway cafes all year
ruleCards.text: A seasonal roadway cafe runs April 1 to November 29 and must be gone by November 30. Since a 2026 law a year-round roadway license exists, at the higher sidewalk rates ($6-$31 per sq ft a year instead of $5-$25). Sidewalk cafes were always year-round.

ruleCards.title: Winter vestibules
ruleCards.text: A storm enclosure at the door is allowed only from November 15 through April 15, needs a permit and may stand no more than 18 inches beyond the building line. Left up after April 15, it is an illegal structure that anyone can report to 311.

ruleCards.title: Light is in the Health Code
ruleCards.text: The Health Code sets light levels: 50 foot-candles where food is prepared, 20 at hand sinks, dishwashing, inside fridges and in the restroom, 10 in dry storage. Bulbs over food must be shatterproof or shielded. Too dark: $100, waived the first time if you fix it.

ruleCards.title: 42 decibels upstairs
ruleCards.text: Music from a business may not exceed 42 decibels measured inside a neighbor's home; one rooftop fan or compressor has the same limit, several together 45. A first music violation is $2,000, reduced to $0 only if a noise consultant certifies the fix.

ruleCards.title: Sidewalk cellar doors
ruleCards.text: Sidewalk cellar doors may stand open during a delivery only while a person guards the opening. The city inspects doors that are bent, wobbly or left open and unprotected. A fall through an open hatch is a claim against whoever kept it.

ruleCards.title: No garbage disposal
ruleCards.text: Food waste grinders are not allowed in NYC businesses, and every business that sends grease down the drain should have a properly sized grease interceptor. Milk and coffee grounds go in the bin, not the sink.

ruleCards.title: Keep the way out clear
ruleCards.text: Every path to an exit must stay clear at all times. Milk crates in the back hallway or a chair in front of the rear door is a Fire Department summons: about $950 the first time and more than double for a repeat within 18 months.

ruleCards.title: More than 30 people: two toilet rooms
ruleCards.text: Plumbing Code: where customers must be given a toilet and the space holds more than 30 people, staff included, it needs separate facilities. Two single all-gender rooms satisfy that. The rule bites when a space is built or altered, so seat 20 can mean two restrooms.

ruleCards.title: One door is not always enough
ruleCards.text: One exit serves a business room only if the farthest corner is within 75 feet of walking distance once more than 30 people use it (100 feet with sprinklers). A long, narrow storefront can need a second exit with 40 seats.

ruleCards.title: Rules for the outdoor area
ruleCards.text: Outdoor seats count toward the 20-seat restroom line. You may not prepare or store food, utensils or equipment outside, nobody may smoke or vape there, and your pest control contract must be extended to cover the outdoor setup.

ruleCards.title: The unit on the roof has its own permit
ruleCards.text: An air conditioning or refrigeration unit mounted on the roof or hung from the ceiling needs a Fire Department permit: $105 per compressor, renewed every year. A small floor unit under five horsepower with ordinary refrigerant is exempt.

ruleCards.title: What a real ramp takes
ruleCards.text: A ramp may rise 1 inch per foot of length at most, must be 36 inches wide and have a landing at top and bottom. A 7-inch step needs 7 feet. Only an existing building with no room may go steeper: 1:10 for a rise up to 6 inches, 1:8 up to 3 inches.

ruleCards.title: No hot water, no service
ruleCards.text: Every hand wash sink needs hot and cold running water. Without it: a critical violation, $300-$350, and the Health Department can close the shop until the water runs hot. A dead water heater is an emergency, not a repair for next week.

ruleCards.title: Backflow test every year
ruleCards.text: If your water service has a backflow preventer, a state-certified tester working for a licensed master plumber must test it every year and file the report with DEP. No report means a summons: fines run from $700 to $10,000.

ruleCards.title: Fire extinguisher tags
ruleCards.text: Every extinguisher needs an FDNY tag renewed each year by an approved company, plus a monthly check you record on the back of the tag. A missing or expired tag: $600, or $300 if you fix it and admit it, up to $1,000 if you ignore the summons.

ruleCards.title: The 2-hour rule
ruleCards.text: When the power or a fridge fails, keep the doors shut. Cold food that stayed above 41°F for less than 2 hours may be chilled again and sold. More than 2 hours, or you do not know how long: throw it out.

ruleCards.title: Tell the Health Department
ruleCards.text: After a fire, flood or power outage that may have left food above 41°F, the owner must notify the Health Department immediately (Health Code §81.43). The Department can order service stopped while the hazard lasts.

ruleCards.title: Con Edison pays for spoiled stock, sometimes
ruleCards.text: If a failure in Con Edison's local network leaves you dark for more than 12 hours in 24, a business can claim up to $12,900 of spoiled perishables. File within 30 days with an itemized list and proof. Storm outages are not covered.

ruleCards.title: After 72 hours without power
ruleCards.text: State law: when a widespread outage lasts 72 hours or more, the utility must reimburse small businesses for food spoiled by lack of refrigeration. You need an itemized list and proof of loss within 14 days. Photograph everything before you throw it out.

ruleCards.title: Cards without internet
ruleCards.text: A Square register can take cards offline, but the payments must upload within 72 hours and you carry the loss if a card is later declined. Set a per-sale limit, and never log out or reset the device before it reconnects.

ruleCards.title: Your water depends on your block
ruleCards.text: New York City water averages 1.8 grains of hardness per gallon, very soft. Where Croton water is blended in it can reach 7 grains: the same softening cartridge then lasts a quarter as long. Ask DEP which supply feeds your address.

ruleCards.title: What voids the warranty
ruleCards.text: Espresso machine warranties last about 12-13 months and exclude scale and bad water. Most are void unless a certified technician installed the machine with water treatment. Keep the install invoice and the filter change log.

ruleCards.title: Ice is food
ruleCards.text: Makers ask for an ice machine to be cleaned and sanitized about every 6 months. Mold or slime inside counts as a dirty food-contact surface: $200-$300 and 5 to 8 points. A neglected machine lasts 4-5 years instead of 7-10.

ruleCards.title: Sanitizing dishes
ruleCards.text: By hand: wash, rinse, then sanitize in 170°F water for 30 seconds or in a chemical solution. A dish machine must reach 160°F at the dish surface or use a chemical sanitizer with a test kit: no kit, or an unused one, is a $200 violation.

ruleCards.title: Selling beans by weight
ruleCards.text: A scale used to sell goods by weight must be inspected and sealed by the city every year: $20 for a scale up to 33 lb. A scale that fails may not be used. Pre-packed bags with a printed net weight need no scale.

ruleCards.title: Equipment and taxes
ruleCards.text: Equipment is not lost money on your tax return: under Section 179 a business can deduct the full cost in the year it starts using it, up to $2,560,000 in 2026. Without that choice it is written off over 5 years.

ruleCards.title: Leasing a machine
ruleCards.text: A leased espresso machine costs about $217 a month per $10,000 at 11% over 5 years, and New York sales tax of 8.875% is due on each payment. Before you sign, read who owes the remaining payments if the shop closes.

ruleCards.title: Con Edison pays for upgrades
ruleCards.text: Con Edison's small business program covers up to 70% of the cost of efficient lighting, refrigeration and controls for customers under 300 kW. Apply first: work started before the offer letter does not qualify.

ruleCards.title: Used equipment
ruleCards.text: Used restaurant equipment sells 30-70% below new, with a warranty of 0 to 3 months. When you sell it yourself you get 10-30% of what you paid. Buy used from a closing cafe; never count on equipment to get your money back.

ruleCards.title: When the gas is locked
ruleCards.text: After a leak the utility shuts the gas and will not restore it until a licensed plumber repairs the piping, the Buildings Department signs off and the lines pass a pressure test. New York restaurants have waited 2 to 7 months. All-electric shops are spared.

ruleCards.title: Water shut-offs
ruleCards.text: For planned street work the city posts notices at least 24 hours ahead: water goes off in the morning and returns by the end of the workday. A main break comes with no notice: the city had 552 of them in fiscal 2025.

ruleCards.title: The free espresso machine
ruleCards.text: A roaster may lend or discount the machine if you buy its coffee: typically 20-40 lb a week. The rent is built into the bean price. Fall below the minimum or leave early and the machine is no longer free. Read the exit terms.

ruleCards.title: Sales tax on repairs
ruleCards.text: In New York, installing, servicing and repairing equipment is a taxable service: add 8.875% to every repair bill in the city. A true capital improvement to the building is not taxed, but the contractor needs a signed certificate (Form ST-124).

ruleCards.title: One machine, one circuit
ruleCards.text: A two-group espresso machine needs its own 20-amp, 208-240 volt circuit; a three-group needs 30 amps. Grinders go on separate circuits. Plugging an oven or a second machine into a shared line trips the breaker at the rush.

ruleCards.title: The demand charge
ruleCards.text: On Con Edison's general large rate, which starts at roughly 10 kW of demand, a business pays for its peak as well as its use: up to $36.50 per kW of the highest weekday demand in summer. Heating everything at once sets the bill for the month.

ruleCards.title: Water is the most common insurance claim
ruleCards.text: Water and freezing damage is the most common small-business claim: 22% of claims in 2020-2024, $34,600 on average. Burglary and theft is 20%. An insurer can refuse a leak that comes from lack of maintenance.

ruleCards.title: No foam
ruleCards.text: Single-use foam cups, clamshells, plates and trays have been banned in the city since 2019. Fines run $150, $250, then $500 per notice in 12 months. A non-chain shop under $500,000 of revenue a year can apply for a hardship waiver.

ruleCards.title: Straws and stirrers
ruleCards.text: Plastic stirrers and splash sticks: banned since November 2021; use wood. Plastic straws: only when a customer asks, and you must keep some in stock for people who need one. Fines $100, $200, then $400.

ruleCards.title: Skip the Stuff
ruleCards.text: For takeout and delivery, no utensils, napkins, condiment packets or extra containers unless the customer asks. A self-serve station in the shop is fine. Fines since July 1, 2024: $50, $150, then $250.

ruleCards.title: The sliced bagel rule
ruleCards.text: A dozen bagels to take away: no sales tax. A plain bagel eaten in the shop, or one toasted or with cream cheese even to go: 8.875%. Any sandwich is taxed. Sell a taxed and an untaxed item for one price and the whole price is taxed.

ruleCards.title: The 5-cent bottle
ruleCards.text: Sell bottled water or soda and you charge a 5-cent deposit, post two signs and take back empties of the brands and sizes you sell: at least 240 per person a day, in all open hours except the first and last.

ruleCards.title: No CBD in the cup
ruleCards.text: The Health Department treats CBD and cannabis in food or drink as adulteration. The product is thrown out, the summons can reach $1,200 and the points count toward your grade. Sealed CBD goods need a state retail license.

ruleCards.title: Milk on the counter
ruleCards.text: Cold food may sit out without refrigeration for up to 4 hours only if it carries a label with the time it came out and the time to throw it away. After that it is discarded, never put back in the fridge.

ruleCards.title: Bottling for other shops
ruleCards.text: Your city permit covers what you sell at your own counter. Bottling cold brew or roasting coffee to sell to other stores needs a state Article 20-C food processing license: $175 for a business with up to ten full-time employees, $400 otherwise. Allow 60 days and an inspection.

ruleCards.title: Labels on what you pack ahead
ruleCards.text: Since November 12, 2026 food you make, pack ahead and sell on the premises needs a label naming any of the 9 major allergens in it. Food wrapped after the order is exempt. State penalty: up to $600, then up to $1,200, and each package counts.

ruleCards.title: Chains only: calories, salt, sugar
ruleCards.text: A shop that is one of 15 or more under the same name must post calories, a salt warning and, since October 4, 2025, an icon on items with 50 g or more of added sugars. Each is a $200 summons. One independent shop is exempt.

ruleCards.title: Small trash, shared carter
ruleCards.text: A business that throws out less than 20 gallons of garbage a week may share a private carter's service with a neighbor, under a written contract with its own decal. A cafe with 200 orders a day is far above that.

ruleCards.title: Free drinks and use tax
ruleCards.text: Taxable goods you bought tax-free for resale and then gave away, such as a bottled soda for a guest or a staff meal, owe use tax on your cost. A two-for-one special does not.

ruleCards.title: Protected time off (2026)
ruleCards.text: NYC law: 40 hours of safe and sick leave a year, earned at 1 hour per 30 worked, plus 32 unpaid hours available from the first day (since February 22, 2026). No doctor's note for 3 days or less, and staff need not find their own cover.

ruleCards.title: The fifth employee
ruleCards.text: Sick leave turns from unpaid to paid at five employees. With 1 to 4 workers and net income under $1 million, the 40 hours are unpaid but protected; with 5 to 99 they are paid at the regular rate. Part-timers count.

ruleCards.title: Paid Family Leave
ruleCards.text: A worker can take up to 12 weeks of Paid Family Leave at 67% of pay, up to $1,228.53 a week in 2026, paid by the insurer. You must hold the job and keep any health coverage going. You pay nothing, but you are short one person.

ruleCards.title: Jury duty
ruleCards.text: A worker called for jury duty cannot be fired or punished for serving. Employers with more than 10 employees pay the first 3 days, up to $72 a day; smaller shops need not pay, but must give the time off.

ruleCards.title: When someone leaves
ruleCards.text: When anyone leaves, for any reason, hand over two papers within 5 working days: a letter with the last day and the date benefits end, and the state Record of Employment (form IA 12.3) so they can claim unemployment.

ruleCards.title: Unemployment claims raise your rate
ruleCards.text: Benefits paid to people you let go are charged to your account and raise your state rate: 1.7% to 9.5% in 2026 against 4.1% for a new employer. A quit without good cause or a firing for misconduct is not charged, if you answer the state's notice on time.

ruleCards.title: Six years of records
ruleCards.text: Wage claims in New York reach back six years and are doubled. Keep schedules, punches, pay stubs, tip sheets and signed pay notices that long. With no records, the worker's own account of the hours is what counts.

ruleCards.title: Tips paid by card
ruleCards.text: Card tips belong to the staff. New York lets you take off only the card company's own fee on the tip, pro rata (about 2.5 cents on the dollar), and tips must be shown apart from wages on the pay stub.

ruleCards.title: The owner behind the bar
ruleCards.text: An owner or manager may keep a tip handed over for a drink they alone made and served. They may not take anything from the shared jar or the pooled card tips, however many hours they worked the bar.

ruleCards.title: Cannabis off the clock
ruleCards.text: Cannabis is legal for adults in New York. You may not test for it or discipline staff for using it off the clock (Labor Law 201-d). You may act only on specific, visible signs of impairment during a shift.

ruleCards.title: Fingerprint clocks and monitoring
ruleCards.text: You may not require a fingerprint, so a fingerprint time clock must be optional (Labor Law 201-a). If you monitor staff phones, email or internet you must give written notice at hire and post it: $500, $1,000, then $3,000 per offense.

ruleCards.title: Retirement plan at 10 employees
ruleCards.text: From 10 employees and two years in business, a New York employer with no retirement plan must enroll staff in the state Secure Choice IRA and pass on their payroll deductions. Registration deadlines ran from March to July 2026.

ruleCards.title: The credit for tax on tips
ruleCards.text: You pay 7.65% payroll tax on the tips your staff report. Form 8846 gives it back as a credit against your income tax when their wage is $5.15 an hour or more. On $2,000 of monthly tips that is $153 a month. Many owners never claim it.

ruleCards.title: Minimum wage outlook
ruleCards.text: NYC minimum wage is $17.00 in 2026 and is reported unchanged for January 1, 2027. A City Council bill (Int. 757, March 2026) would phase in $30 by 2030 for large firms, $29 by 2031 for small ones, and end the tipped wage. It is not law.

ruleCards.title: Workers' comp audit
ruleCards.text: Workers' comp is billed on estimated payroll and trued up by an audit after the policy year. Underestimate and a bill follows. Pay a cleaner or handyman who has no insurance of their own and their fee is added to your payroll.

ruleCards.title: Expiring work permits
ruleCards.text: When a work permit expires, re-check documents on Form I-9 Supplement B on that date, not before, and let the worker choose which valid document to show. Checking early is discrimination; missing it risks $288 to $2,861 per form.

ruleCards.title: Free hiring help from the city
ruleCards.text: NYC Workforce1 recruits and screens candidates for businesses at no cost. First Course NYC refunds restaurants half of an apprentice's training wages for the first 6 weeks (up to 210 hours). Few small owners know either exists.

ruleCards.title: Summer Youth Employment Program
ruleCards.text: For six weeks in July and August the city pays young New Yorkers (16 to 24) $17.00 an hour for up to 25 hours a week at host businesses. The host pays nothing but must supervise. Employers sign up between late January and early May.

ruleCards.title: New York Youth Jobs tax credit
ruleCards.text: New York State gives a tax credit of up to $7,500 for hiring an unemployed, at-risk worker aged 16 to 24 full time, or $3,750 part time. The business must be certified by the Labor Department and apply by November 30 of the year.

ruleCards.title: Harassment notice on the wall
ruleCards.text: Every NYC employer must post the city's sexual harassment prevention notice in English and Spanish and hand each new hire the city fact sheet. Yearly training is a city duty from 15 employees and a state duty for every employer.

ruleCards.title: Staff report tips to you
ruleCards.text: A worker who gets $20 or more in tips in a month must report them to you in writing by the 10th of the next month. Card tips you pay out count. A service charge you add to a bill is wages, not a tip, and earns no tip credit.

ruleCards.title: Report every new hire in 20 days
ruleCards.text: New York employers must report each newly hired or rehired employee to the state within 20 calendar days of the first day of work. The penalty is $20 for each employee not reported. Payroll services usually file it for you.

ruleCards.title: Delivery app fees are capped
ruleCards.text: NYC caps what an app may charge a restaurant: 15% for delivery, 5% for basic service, 3% for card processing. Optional 'enhanced' services may add up to 20%, and only if the app also offers the basic plan. Overcharged? The city has won refunds for restaurants.

ruleCards.title: The grade stays in the window
ruleCards.text: A, B or C must hang within five feet of the door where passersby can see it. After a bad re-inspection you may post 'Grade Pending' until your hearing. A missing card costs $500; a removed or covered one costs $1,000.

ruleCards.title: Card surcharges
ruleCards.text: In New York the posted price must already be the full credit card price. The extra may not exceed what your processor charges, and debit cards are excluded. A fee added at the register costs up to $500 per violation.

ruleCards.title: Dogs
ruleCards.text: Only service dogs may come inside a food establishment in NYC. Pet dogs are allowed in outdoor seating if you post the sign and they stay leashed. A dog inside is a critical violation: 5 to 8 points toward your grade and a $200 to $350 fine.

ruleCards.title: What a star is worth
ruleCards.text: A Harvard study of Seattle restaurants: one more Yelp star lifts an independent's revenue 5-9%; chains gain nothing. In 2026, 68% of consumers want at least 4 stars and 31% want 4.5.

ruleCards.title: Room for the line
ruleCards.text: A comfortable line needs about 8.5 sq ft a person. When the line spills out the door, people walk past, and more of them in the cold.

ruleCards.title: Regulars
ruleCards.text: Square's data: a regular brings six times the yearly revenue of a one-time customer, and about 15% of customers come back at least twice in a working week. A cafe is built on a few hundred people, not on the crowd.

ruleCards.title: Split shifts
ruleCards.text: If a worker's day runs more than 10 hours from first clock-in to last clock-out, breaks included, New York's hospitality wage order adds one hour of pay at the minimum wage for that day: $17 in New York City in 2026.

ruleCards.title: Flyers on poles
ruleCards.text: Taping flyers to lampposts, mailboxes or fences is illegal posting: $75 for each flyer, $125 if you ignore the summons. Ten flyers is ten tickets. One new Brooklyn shop was reportedly fined almost $9,000.

ruleCards.title: Congestion Relief Zone
ruleCards.text: Below 60th Street in Manhattan cars pay $9 a day at peak hours; delivery trucks pay $14.40 or $21.60 every time they enter. In year one foot traffic in the zone rose 3.4% against 1.4% for the borough, and truck speeds rose 5.6%.

ruleCards.title: When the power goes out
ruleCards.text: If a failure in Con Edison's local grid leaves you dark for more than 12 hours in a 24-hour period, a business can claim spoiled perishables, up to $12,900, within 30 days. Storm outages are not paid.

ruleCards.title: Outdoor dining, all year
ruleCards.text: Sidewalk cafes may operate all year, and since 2026 roadway cafes may too, under a year-round license with higher fees. The license is $1,050 for four years, or $2,100 for sidewalk and roadway together, plus a yearly fee set by location and size.

ruleCards.title: Smoke days
ruleCards.text: An Air Quality Index above 150 is unhealthy for everyone. In July 2026 Canadian wildfire smoke pushed New York City to 289, second only to June 2023. No law makes you close, but outdoor seats are useless and staff should not work outside.

ruleCards.title: Holiday pay
ruleCards.text: New York law does not require a private employer to pay extra for work on Thanksgiving or Christmas. Time-and-a-half is a custom, not a rule, unless your own handbook promises it. Overtime after 40 hours and the spread-of-hours hour still apply.

ruleCards.title: A corner means two sidewalks
ruleCards.text: On a corner you clear both frontages plus access to the crosswalk and the curb ramp, and you must shovel out the fire hydrant and any bus stop without a shelter. Same clock: 4 hours after daytime snow. A corner shop shovels twice as much.

ruleCards.title: Music and the neighbors
ruleCards.text: You may not use a speaker to draw customers on the sidewalk. Music from a business may not exceed 42 dB(A) inside a neighbor's apartment. A first violation is $2,000, cut to $0 if you fix it and certify the fix, and $8,000 if you ignore it.

ruleCards.title: Fines are under review
ruleCards.text: Executive Order 11 (January 14, 2026) told city agencies to review rules and fines on small businesses and propose cuts, warnings and cure periods. An earlier round changed 116 rules, most of them rarely used. Until a fine is changed, it stands.

ruleCards.title: A broken sidewalk is the owner's to fix
ruleCards.text: When the city marks a sidewalk defect, the property owner has 75 days to repair it. There is no fine, but after 75 days the city may do the work and bill the owner. Most store leases pass sidewalk repairs to the tenant.

ruleCards.title: How points add up
ruleCards.text: Inspectors score each violation by how bad it is: general ones 2-5 points, critical ones 5-10, public health hazards 7 or more, and 28 at the worst level. A total under 14 is an A, 14-27 a B, 28 or more a C.

ruleCards.title: An A means no fines
ruleCards.text: Score under 14 points on an initial inspection and you pay no fines for the scored violations found that day. Signs, smoking and other unscored violations are still fined.

ruleCards.title: Grade Pending
ruleCards.text: Score 14 or more on a re-inspection and the B or C is not final until your hearing. Until then you may post the 'Grade Pending' card the inspector leaves instead of the letter.

ruleCards.title: After a 28
ruleCards.text: Score 28 or more and inspectors keep coming about once a month until you score under 28, or until the Health Department closes the shop for serious and persistent violations.

ruleCards.title: Closed by the Health Department
ruleCards.text: Inspectors close a shop for a hazard that cannot be fixed during the visit, or for no permit. One tracker counted 583 closures at 518 NYC restaurants in a year, about 2.5% of those inspected; mice were cited in 44%.

ruleCards.title: Tickets go to a hearing
ruleCards.text: City tickets are decided at OATH, the city tribunal. You can pay, accept the agency's settlement offer, or contest by phone, online or mail. For fire tickets, proof of the fix by the hearing date halves the fine: $600 becomes $300.

ruleCards.title: Never skip a hearing
ruleCards.text: Miss the hearing and you lose by default at the higher penalty: a $500 grade-card ticket becomes $1,000. Unpaid defaults become court judgments handed to the sheriff or a city marshal. You get one request to reopen.

ruleCards.title: Fix it and pay $0
ruleCards.text: For some first-time violations that are not food-safety hazards, such as a missing sign, the city lets you fix the problem within days, notify the agency and pay $0 (Local Law 80 of 2021).

ruleCards.title: Allergen labels on grab-and-go
ruleCards.text: Since November 12, 2026, food you make, pack and sell in the same shop for takeaway, such as a wrapped sandwich or a cup of overnight oats, needs a label naming its major allergens (Public Health Law §1357).

ruleCards.title: Not in the corner basket
ruleCards.text: Shop trash may never go into public litter baskets or the building's residential pile. You must hire a private carter and post its decal. Agents open bags and look for your receipts: $100 to $300.

ruleCards.title: A-frame signs
ruleCards.text: An A-frame sign may stand no more than 3 feet from your wall. Farther out it is a sidewalk obstruction: about $100 the first time and up to $300 after.

ruleCards.title: Foam, straws and forks
ruleCards.text: Foam cups and containers are banned: $150, then $250, then $500. Plastic straws only on request: $100 to $400. Forks, napkins and sauce packets go into takeout only if the customer asks: $50 to $250.

ruleCards.title: No extra percentages on the menu
ruleCards.text: A place serving food to eat in may not add a percentage to listed prices: a 5% living-wage fee or a 20% administrative charge is illegal. Allowed if disclosed up front: a split-plate charge or a gratuity for parties of 8 or more.

ruleCards.title: No payback for complaints
ruleCards.text: You may not fire, threaten or cut the hours of a worker who complains about pay or safety. The state can fine $1,000 to $10,000, and a court awards the worker up to $20,000 more, plus lost pay.

ruleCards.title: No rent control for shops
ruleCards.text: New York has no commercial rent control and no right to renew a store lease. At renewal the landlord may ask any rent: in 2025 one Brooklyn cafe's rent nearly tripled and another faced $4,000 more a month. Both closed.

ruleCards.title: If you miss the rent
ruleCards.text: The landlord must first serve a written 14-day demand. Then comes a court case; after a judgment a city marshal gives 14 days' notice before changing the locks. Paying everything owed before that stops the eviction.

ruleCards.title: Landlord harassment
ruleCards.text: A landlord may refuse to renew, but may not force you out by cutting services or blocking your door. Commercial tenant harassment carries a civil penalty of $10,000 to $50,000, and you can sue.

ruleCards.title: Beer, wine and decoys
ruleCards.text: A beer and wine license brings the Liquor Authority, which sends underage decoys. A first sale to a minor costs $2,500 to $4,000, up to $10,000 per violation, and repeats can cost the license.

ruleCards.title: Real inspectors do not take cash
ruleCards.text: Real city inspectors show photo ID and never take money on the spot: fines are paid to the city after a hearing. Anyone asking for cash for an inspection, a $92.58 poster or an extinguisher check is running a scam.

ruleCards.title: Hot drinks burn
ruleCards.text: In 2025 a Los Angeles jury awarded $50 million to a delivery driver burned when a hot tea was not secured in its carrier. Lids pressed on, cups seated in the tray and a liability policy are cheap by comparison.

ruleCards.title: Slips and falls
ruleCards.text: Customer slip-and-falls are among the 5 most common restaurant insurance claims and often settle for $10,000 to $50,000. Mats at the door, wet-floor signs and a dated mopping log are what your insurer's lawyer asks for.

ruleCards.title: Anyone can call 311
ruleCards.text: Anyone can file a 311 complaint, without a name, and agencies send inspectors. A 2026 City Council bill would stop inspections after 3 unverified anonymous complaints in 6 months; it has not passed.

ruleCards.title: Wage suits come late and large
ruleCards.text: Wage claims reach back 6 years and usually arrive after a worker leaves. NYC restaurant wage suits settled for $725,000 to $1.75 million in 2025; Starbucks paid $35.5 million to about 15,000 city workers plus $3.4 million in penalties.

ruleCards.title: Waste zones keep rolling out
ruleCards.text: On October 16, 2026 four more commercial waste zones took effect: Brooklyn East, Manhattan Northeast, Queens West and Manhattan West. Inside a zone you may sign only with one of its 3 authorized carters.

ruleCards.title: Check the name first
ruleCards.text: Search trademarks before you print the name. A Michigan cafe sued by a national coffee chain was told a court fight could cost $50,000; it renamed for about $5,000. Another owner got 10 days to destroy branded goods.

ruleCards.title: Your grade follows you online
ruleCards.text: Under a rule in force since November 15, 2025, delivery apps must link to the city's inspection lookup. A B or C is now one tap away from your menu, not only in the window.

ruleCards.title: The city emails before it inspects
ruleCards.text: Since 2025 restaurants get two emails before a health inspection, the first 1 to 5 months ahead, with the checklist the inspector uses. The exact day stays unknown. Keep the email address on your permit current.

ruleCards.title: A cure erases the fine, not the points
ruleCards.text: Fixing a curable violation within days can bring its fine to $0, but the points stay in your inspection score and the grade does not change.

ruleCards.title: Hearings in your language
ruleCards.text: Every OATH hearing offers a free interpreter, and the city's Business Owner Bill of Rights promises information in languages other than English. A 2026 audit still found gaps in interpretation during restaurant inspections.

ruleCards.title: Rules change every year
ruleCards.text: In July 2026 the city announced more than 50 red-tape reforms, 25 of them for food businesses: one food-safety fine fell from $600 to $500 and a permit was abolished. Check fines and permits again before every season.

ruleCards.title: Sales tax dates
ruleCards.text: New York's sales tax quarters end in February, May, August and November, and the return is due on the 20th of March, June, September and December. A shop taking $51,000 a month owes about $13,600 each time.

ruleCards.title: A reward for filing on time
ruleCards.text: File and pay your quarterly sales tax return on time and New York lets you keep 5% of the tax, up to $200 a quarter. File one day late and the credit is gone, replaced by a penalty of at least $50.

ruleCards.title: An LLC does not shield sales tax
ruleCards.text: Every member of an LLC can be held personally liable for 100% of the sales tax the business owes (NY Tax Law §§1131, 1133). The debt follows you after the shop closes, and bankruptcy does not erase tax you collected.

ruleCards.title: When tax goes unpaid
ruleCards.text: New York files a tax warrant, then levies bank accounts and can take up to 10% of your wages. At $10,000 of past-due tax it can suspend your driver's license after a 60-day notice. In June 2026 it seized a Manhattan restaurant.

ruleCards.title: Money spent before opening
ruleCards.text: Costs before opening day are not a normal deduction. You may deduct $5,000 in year one, less every dollar over $50,000 (nothing at $55,000), and the rest over 180 months. Pre-opening rent and wages count; equipment is depreciated.

ruleCards.title: Nobody withholds tax for an owner
ruleCards.text: Estimated income tax is due April 15, June 15, September 15 and January 15. Pay at least 100% of last year's tax (110% if income was over $150,000) and there is no penalty; otherwise the IRS charges 7% a year on what was short.

ruleCards.title: The IRS already knows your card sales
ruleCards.text: Your card processor reports every dollar of card sales on Form 1099-K, with no minimum. An auditor starts from that number and can estimate cash sales by watching your register for one day and applying the ratio to three years.

ruleCards.title: Card money arrives later
ruleCards.text: Square pays out the next business day and sends nothing on Saturday: Friday, Saturday and Sunday sales arrive on Monday, or Tuesday after a bank holiday. Instant transfers cost 1.95% of every dollar moved.

ruleCards.title: Disputed card payments
ruleCards.text: When a customer disputes a charge the processor pulls the money back at once. You get 7 days to answer and the bank can take up to 90 days to decide. Square charges no dispute fee, but if you lose, the processing fee is not returned.

ruleCards.title: Card surcharges
ruleCards.text: In New York you may pass on your real card cost only if the higher card price is posted in dollars before the sale. A surprise fee line on the receipt costs up to $500 per violation (General Business Law §518).

ruleCards.title: What an SBA loan asks of you
ruleCards.text: An SBA 7(a) loan needs about 10% of the project in your own cash and a personal guarantee from every owner of 20% or more. Since March 1, 2026 every owner must be a U.S. citizen. Up to $250,000 the rate may reach prime + 6%: 13% today.

ruleCards.title: The SBA guaranty fee
ruleCards.text: From October 2026 the SBA charges 2% of the guaranteed part of loans up to $150,000 and 3% up to $700,000, and lenders pass it on. On a $100,000 loan guaranteed at 85% that is $1,700 before you buy a single cup.

ruleCards.title: Merchant cash advance
ruleCards.text: A cash advance is not a loan: you sell future card sales. $40,000 today for $54,000 taken as 15% of each day's card sales works out near 90% a year. New York makes funders disclose the APR in writing; read it before signing.

ruleCards.title: Personal guarantee
ruleCards.text: A personal guarantee puts your own savings behind the business. An SBA lender must also take a lien on your home if you own 25% or more of its value and the business assets do not fully cover the loan.

ruleCards.title: Walking away from a lease
ruleCards.text: A New York commercial landlord has no duty to look for a new tenant after you leave (Holy Properties v. Kenneth Cole, 1995). The space can stay empty while the rent for the rest of the lease is billed to you and your guarantor.

ruleCards.title: Selling the shop: the tax department comes first
ruleCards.text: A buyer must notify the state at least 10 days before paying. If the seller owes sales tax, the state claims it from the price. The seller must also collect 8.875% sales tax on the equipment and furniture sold.

ruleCards.title: Your lease after you sell
ruleCards.text: Selling the shop does not end your lease. Unless the landlord signs a written release, the seller and the seller's guarantor stay liable for the rent if the buyer stops paying. Negotiate the release before you sign the lease.

ruleCards.title: What bankruptcy does and does not erase
ruleCards.text: Bankruptcy can erase personally guaranteed rent and loans, but not sales tax you collected or payroll tax you withheld. Filing Chapter 7 costs $338. In New York City up to $204,825 of equity in your home is protected.

ruleCards.title: Wages and the LLC
ruleCards.text: In New York the ten largest owners of an LLC are personally liable for unpaid wages (LLC Law §609(c)). Close the shop owing a final payroll and the staff can collect it from you after giving written notice within 180 days.

ruleCards.title: What the basic policy leaves out
ruleCards.text: A standard business policy does not pay for a flood, a sewer backup, or a power cut that starts outside your shop and the milk that spoils in it. Lost income is covered only after a 72-hour wait. Each gap is a separate add-on.

ruleCards.title: Insurance is billed twice
ruleCards.text: Premiums start as estimates. After the policy year the insurer audits your real payroll for workers' comp and your real sales for liability. Grow faster than you guessed and a bill for the difference arrives.

ruleCards.title: The S corporation in New York City
ruleCards.text: The S corporation saves less here than online advice says. New York City does not recognize it and taxes its profit at 8.85%, against 4% for an LLC, where a credit erases the tax on profit under about $100,000.

ruleCards.title: Closing has paperwork
ruleCards.text: To close: a final sales tax return within 20 days, a final state payroll return within 30 days of the last wages, final federal returns and W-2s, and $60 to dissolve the LLC. Skip it and penalties grow on a business that is gone.

ruleCards.title: Forgiven debt is income
ruleCards.text: If a lender forgives $20,000 you could not repay, the IRS counts $20,000 as your income (Form 1099-C), unless you were insolvent at that moment or the debt was wiped out in bankruptcy.

ruleCards.title: Your own health insurance
ruleCards.text: Leave your job and its health plan goes too. In 2026 the cheapest silver plan on New York's marketplace costs $807 a month for one adult in Brooklyn, Queens and the Bronx, before any subsidy.

ruleCards.title: Gift card money
ruleCards.text: Money from a gift card is not earned until the card is used. In New York a balance left untouched for five years must be handed to the State Comptroller's unclaimed funds office, and cards sold since 2022 may not expire or lose value to fees.

ruleCards.title: A city return even when you owe nothing
ruleCards.text: An unincorporated business in New York City with gross income over $95,000 must file an Unincorporated Business Tax return even when the credit wipes the tax out. A cafe passes $95,000 of sales in its second month.

ruleCards.title: The city loan fund
ruleCards.text: NYC Future Fund lends $25,000-$500,000 at 7.5% for up to five years with a 3% fee, but only to businesses with 12 months of history and a filed tax return. It can refinance an expensive loan in year two; it cannot fund your opening.

ruleCards.title: Profit is taxed at your family's rate
ruleCards.text: A single-member LLC's profit lands on your personal return on top of a spouse's salary, so each extra dollar is taxed at the household's top rate plus 14.1% self-employment tax. A first-year loss works the other way and cuts the family's tax.

ruleCards.title: Shortages are the owner's loss
ruleCards.text: A short cash drawer, a broken grinder or a customer who walked out may not be taken from wages in New York, not even by asking the worker to pay it back separately (Labor Law §193). Deducted money is owed back double.

ruleCards.title: Unemployment tax hits early in the year
ruleCards.text: New York unemployment tax is 4.1% on the first $17,600 of each worker's pay and federal tax 0.6% on the first $7,000. So the cost falls in the first months of the year or of a new hire, then stops, and starts again in January.

ruleCards.title: Hidden sales cannot be sold or borrowed against
ruleCards.text: A buyer's bank and an SBA lender value your shop from tax returns. Cash that never reached the books earns no loan and no sale price: at 2 times earnings, each hidden $10,000 of yearly profit cuts about $20,000 off the price.

ruleCards.title: Your lease ends when it ends
ruleCards.text: A commercial tenant in New York has no right to renew and no cap on the next rent. In 2025 Brooklyn cafes were offered two to three times their old rent. An option to renew exists only if it is written into the lease.

ruleCards.title: Gas comes back slowly
ruleCards.text: After a utility shuts off a building's gas, service returns only after a licensed plumber, a Buildings permit, a pressure test and an inspection. One Brooklyn cafe was dark for more than 8 months over a $3,000 repair.

ruleCards.title: Card fees must be posted as prices
ruleCards.text: Since February 11, 2024 a New York seller that charges more for cards must post the card price (or both prices) and may not add more than its processor charges. Penalty: up to $500 per violation.

ruleCards.title: Space you may not use
ruleCards.text: A yard, basement or roof not covered by the Certificate of Occupancy can be ordered vacated after a single complaint. Yaffa Cafe lost a 100-seat garden it had used for 30 years.

ruleCards.title: The step at the door
ruleCards.text: One step at the entrance is enough for a federal accessibility lawsuit. One plaintiffs' firm has filed about 600 in New York; coffee shops are frequent targets. Settling usually costs less than defending.

ruleCards.title: Sales tax seizure
ruleCards.text: For unpaid sales tax New York files a warrant and can seize the business: a notice on the door, new locks, an auction. A Brooklyn cafe was padlocked twice over $66,000. Returns are due March 20, June 20, September 20 and December 20.

ruleCards.title: Power outages and insurance
ruleCards.text: A standard policy excludes a power failure that starts off your premises. Lost sales and spoiled stock are paid only with a utility-services endorsement and spoilage coverage, often limited to $2,500-$25,000.

ruleCards.title: Fines can be erased
ruleCards.text: Score under 14 points on re-inspection and the penalties from that inspection are waived. New restaurants can book a consultative visit with no grade and no fines: $100 before the first graded inspection.

ruleCards.title: Wage indexing
ruleCards.text: The minimum wage is indexed to Northeast inflation from 2027, with off-ramps. For 2027 an off-ramp was met: the rate stays $17.00 in New York City on January 1, 2027. The next rate is announced by October 1 each year.

ruleCards.title: Pre-opening costs and tax
ruleCards.text: Only $5,000 of start-up costs is deductible in the first year, and nothing at once when they exceed $55,000. The rest is spread over 180 months. Rent paid before opening day is a start-up cost.

ruleCards.title: Bins, not bags
ruleCards.text: Since March 1, 2024 every business that sets trash on the curb must use bins with secure lids. Fines: $50, $100, then $200. Sidewalk and 18 inches of gutter must be kept clean.

ruleCards.title: Skip the Stuff
ruleCards.text: Since July 31, 2023 take-out and delivery orders may not include utensils, napkins or condiment packets unless the customer asks. Fines: $50, $150, then $250 within 12 months.

ruleCards.title: The first year is not the dangerous one
ruleCards.text: A study of 81,000 independent restaurants found 17% failed in year one - not 90%. An Ohio study found 26% in year one and 59% within three years: shops die when the opening money is gone.

ruleCards.title: Where a cart may stand
ruleCards.text: Next to the curb, at least 20 ft from a building entrance and 10 ft from a crosswalk, subway entrance or driveway, on a sidewalk at least 12 ft wide. Civil fines up to $250.

ruleCards.title: Every cart sleeps at a commissary
ruleCards.text: A permitted cart or truck must be cleaned, serviced and stored at a Health Department-approved commissary or depot. No commissary contract, no permit.

ruleCards.title: No selling at a meter
ruleCards.text: Food trucks may not sell while parked at a metered space (34 RCNY 4-08(h)(8)). Courts confirmed it in 2012. Expect tickets and tows.

ruleCards.title: Street vending fines are civil now
ruleCards.text: A 2025 law made most vending offenses civil: up to $250 for placement, up to $1,000 for vending without a license. Sanitation can still remove the setup.

ruleCards.title: Tell the community board first
ruleCards.text: Any on-premises liquor application in NYC needs 30 days' notice to the community board first. The board's vote is advisory, but its stipulations often end up in your license.

ruleCards.title: The 500-foot rule
ruleCards.text: A full liquor license near three or more bars within 500 ft needs a public-interest finding. Beer and wine only places are exempt.

ruleCards.title: Temporary permit while you wait
ruleCards.text: The SLA can issue a 180-day temporary permit while your license is pending: $640 for wine and liquor, $128 for beer only. You may not sell a drop before it is in hand.

ruleCards.title: Wine needs food
ruleCards.text: A Restaurant Wine license ($960 for two years in NYC plus $100 filing) requires a kitchen and a real menu. A pastry counter usually is not enough.

ruleCards.title: The city taxes your license too
ruleCards.text: NYC adds a tax equal to 25% of your annual state license fee, billed by the Department of Finance and due June 25.

ruleCards.title: One sale to a minor
ruleCards.text: First sale to a minor: $2,500-$4,000 civil penalty, up to $10,000. The licensee pays even if a new employee made the sale.

ruleCards.title: Markets need their own permit
ruleCards.text: Your cafe permit covers your storefront only. Street fairs and markets need a $70 Temporary Food Service Establishment Permit and a certified supervisor on site.

ruleCards.title: Raw juice needs a warning
ruleCards.text: Juice you press and bottle for later sale must carry the unpasteurized warning label. Missing labels are cited at $400-$600.

ruleCards.title: Hot food means a hood
ruleCards.text: Grease-producing cooking needs a Type I hood, a duct to the roof and a wet-chemical system installed under FDNY inspection, plus a $70 FDNY cooking permit.

ruleCards.title: Ventless ovens are not automatic
ruleCards.text: High-speed ventless ovens clean their own smoke, but NYC's DOB and FDNY decide whether one is allowed without a hood.

ruleCards.title: Bakeries can answer to the state
ruleCards.text: A mostly wholesale bakery is licensed by the State Department of Agriculture and Markets; a mostly retail one by the city Health Department. Let the state permit lapse and the city can close you.

ruleCards.title: Propane needs a certificate
ruleCards.text: On a cart or truck, only a holder of the FDNY G-23 Certificate of Fitness may hook up propane over one pound. Trucks also need a $105 FDNY permit.

ruleCards.title: Wine to go, by the glass only
ruleCards.text: Licensed places may sell drinks to go through 2030, but only by the glass with a substantial food order; sealed bottles to go are not allowed under SLA guidance.

ruleCards.title: Outdoor drinks need a second approval
ruleCards.text: A DOT sidewalk cafe license does not cover alcohol. After DOT issues it, you file an alteration with the SLA within 60 days and serve outside only once the SLA approves.

ruleCards.title: Shared kitchen, your own permit
ruleCards.text: Renting time in a shared kitchen does not cover you: each business needs its own Food Service Establishment permit, and the kitchen may not rent to anyone without one.

ruleCards.title: Some streets are closed to carts
ruleCards.text: The Health Department publishes restricted streets by borough, day and hour where food vending is barred. Fines start at $50; general vending is barred in most of Midtown.

ruleCards.title: Vendors take their own course
ruleCards.text: Every cart or truck worker needs a $50 two-year license and the $53 Food Protection Course for Mobile Vendors with an exam. Fail and you pay again.

ruleCards.title: Incubator bakers pay no state fee
ruleCards.text: New York waives the $400 Article 20-C food processing license fee for two years for a first-time applicant working in a kitchen incubator.

ruleCards.title: Sandwiches are tavern food
ruleCards.text: For the SLA a restaurant serves full entree-style meals from a chef-run kitchen; a tavern must serve at least soups and sandwiches. A cafe with toasties usually applies for Tavern Wine.

ruleCards.title: Carts have a size limit
ruleCards.text: A sidewalk food cart may be at most about 5 ft wide and 10 ft long including wheels and signs, parked with its long side along the curb. Trucks are exempt from the size rule.

ruleCards.title: Station cafes pay a share
ruleCards.text: Transit kiosks and cafes are licensed by MTA Real Estate: a one-year Grand Central Madison pastry and coffee stall pays 15% of gross sales; larger station cafes pay base rent plus a share above a sales threshold.

ruleCards.title: The apps keep your customers
ruleCards.text: NYC tried to make delivery apps share diners' names and emails with restaurants. Courts held the law unconstitutional in 2024, so delivery customers stay the app's, not yours.

ruleCards.title: Selling juice wholesale changes the rules
ruleCards.text: Juice you bottle for your own customers needs a full label and warning. Sell bottles to other shops and the federal Juice HACCP rule applies, even if the juice never leaves New York.

ruleCards.title: Four hours to clear the snow
ruleCards.text: Snow stops 7am-5pm: clear a 4 ft path within 4 hours. Stops 5-9pm: within 14 hours. Stops overnight: by 11am. Ice you cannot lift gets sand or salt. Tickets: $100, $150, then $250.

ruleCards.title: Storm in progress
ruleCards.text: In New York nobody is liable for ice while the storm is still on and for a reasonable time after. A court found 5 hours reasonable; 12 hours after the storm with a freeze was not.

ruleCards.title: Free rent for the build-out
ruleCards.text: NYC restaurant leases often give 3-6 months of free base rent for construction, up to 12 for a heavy job. The clock usually starts at signing, not when your permits arrive: negotiate it.

ruleCards.title: Check the gas before you sign
ruleCards.text: In a 2017 survey 82% of restaurants had a gas delay: 68 days on average, up to a year, about $140,000 lost each. Con Edison checks gas at an address before you sign. An espresso bar needs none.

ruleCards.title: Costs before opening are not all deductible
ruleCards.text: Rent and other costs before the doors open are start-up costs: $5,000 can be deducted in the first year (less above $50,000), the rest over 15 years.
